mcqs.question: A process has three threads, all runnable. On a machine with a single CPU core, how does the OS scheduler treat them?
options: It ignores two of them until the process is scheduled again
It only schedules one representative thread per process, regardless of how many are runnable
It requires the process to pick which thread runs, since the OS can't see inside a process
It schedules all three as independent runnable entities that time-slice the single core, exactly like separate processes would
mcqs.explanation: The OS scheduler operates on threads, not processes — each runnable thread, regardless of which process it belongs to, competes independently for CPU time. The OS has full visibility into a process's threads; nothing is hidden from it or delegated to the process itself.

mcqs.question: Thread A allocates memory on the heap and writes a value into it. Can thread B, in the same process, read that value directly?
options: No — heap memory is always private to the thread that allocated it
Only if thread A explicitly sends it through a pipe or socket
Yes — the heap is shared across all threads in the same process, so thread B can read it directly through a shared pointer
Only after the process calls fork() to share the memory
mcqs.explanation: The heap is one of the resources shared by every thread in a process, so any thread can read or write memory another thread allocated there, given a pointer to it — no IPC mechanism needed. That direct sharing is also exactly why unsynchronized concurrent access to it is dangerous.

mcqs.question: A design choice uses multiple threads within one process instead of multiple separate processes, specifically to avoid IPC overhead when sharing a cache. What has it implicitly traded away?
options: Fault isolation — a crash or bad pointer in any one thread can now corrupt or take down the whole process
Nothing — threads provide the same isolation guarantees as processes
The ability to run on multiple CPU cores
The ability to share the cache at all
mcqs.explanation: Threads share an address space, so they trade away the crash/memory isolation that separate processes provide — a fault in one thread can corrupt shared state for all of them. Threads can absolutely use multiple cores and are precisely how the cache gets shared cheaply.

mcqs.question: Two threads both run `counter++` on a shared integer with no locking, a million times each. What's the most likely outcome, and why?
options: The final value is unpredictable and usually less than 2 million, because the increment isn't atomic and updates can be lost when both threads read-modify-write concurrently
The final value is always exactly 2 million, since integer addition is a single CPU instruction
The program crashes, since concurrent writes to the same variable are illegal
The final value is always exactly 1 million, since the second thread's writes are always ignored
mcqs.explanation: counter++ is actually read-modify-write, not one atomic step, so two threads can both read the same old value before either writes back, silently losing one increment — a classic race condition. It doesn't crash, and there's no fixed guaranteed result; that unpredictability is exactly the bug.

mcqs.question: A server under a traffic spike starts spawning a brand-new thread for every incoming request with no upper bound. What's the realistic failure mode as load keeps increasing?
options: The server automatically converts excess threads into queued requests with no downside
Nothing — threads are cheap enough that thread count is never a practical limit

Address space and OS thread-count limits get exhausted, and additional runnable threads beyond core count add scheduling overhead without adding real parallelism, degrading rather than improving throughput
CPU usage stays flat regardless of thread count, so this is always safe
mcqs.explanation: Each thread reserves real per-thread resources (stack space, kernel bookkeeping), and unbounded thread creation under load can hit real limits while also causing excessive context-switch overhead once runnable threads outnumber cores — exactly why production systems use bounded thread pools instead.
